items.title: Game over? How playing Grand Theft Auto VI is affecting elite athletes’ performances | Sean Ingle
items.summary:
Burning the midnight oil playing video games is not ideal preparation for professional sport – but it’s not all bad

“They miss games, the cheque’s still clearing. And you’re trying to tell me they got this kind of addiction to a video game that they sitting there with their thumbs looking like Donald Trump?” That was EPSN’s Stephen A Smith, one of the US’s most provocative and influential sports pundits, spitting fire and fury last week after hearing that so many NBA and NFL stars were absorbed in Grand Theft Auto VI.

Smith was hardly an outlier. Other pundits, as well as some Manchester United fans, also questioned Bryan Mbeumo’s focus and professionalism after he posted an image of GTA VI and the word “historique” after midnight on Thursday. Meanwhile before last weekend’s Premier League games, the Odd Sport social media account predicted that Chelsea, Brighton and Manchester City would all lose. Why? Because their younger squads might be more focused on Vice City than their opponents, and therefore play with less intensity as a result. By Monday that forecast had been liked tens of thousands of times.

Continue reading...

Latest greyhound racing blow is a wake-up call with new five-year plan keeping RSPCA on side for now

Britain’s greyhound racing industry woke up on Monday to the news that the Racing Post, the daily trade newspaper that has carried extensive coverage of the sport since its launch in 1986, will drop both editorial and greyhound racecards in its print edition from 10 December.

items.title: ‘I can’t play games just for fun’: meet Javokhir Sindarov, the 20-year-old happy warrior moving for chess’s biggest prize
items.summary:
In an exclusive interview with the Guardian ahead of the most important match of his life, the Uzbek prodigy talks Messi, GTA VI and the competitive streak he can’t switch off

Javokhir Sindarov has a problem. The fast-rising 20-year-old Uzbek grandmaster, who is challenging for the world chess championship over the next three weeks in Switzerland, can’t stop playing for keeps. Even when he is off the clock and meant to be relaxing with friends, a compulsion to win takes hold. His preferred escape is Counter-Strike, the tactical first-person shooter that has become one of the world’s most popular esports. But he also plays EA Sports FC (née Fifa), the all-conquering soccer kickabout, and approaches both with the same seriousness of purpose that has propelled him toward the pinnacle of his day job.

“I’m the guy who can’t play games just for fun,” Sindarov tells the Guardian less than 48 hours before Tuesday’s world championship opener in Geneva, smiling at the absurdity of it. “If I play something, I always try to learn, trying to become better.”

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘I can’t play games just for fun’: meet Javokhir Sindarov, the 20-year-old happy warrior moving for chess’s biggest prize

Unai Emery has insisted he will not alter his plans for Aston Villa’s Champions League game at ­Galatasaray on Tuesday night on account of concerns about the state of the pitch. The Turkish champions hastily moved Saturday’s home fixture from Rams Park after starting emergency repairs to the surface this month. The Villa defender Ian Maatsen said he and his teammates were aware the pitch was in a “bad condition”.

Villa were informed by Uefa last week that they would be unable to train at the venue the day before the Champions League game in order to give the pitch maximum time to recover after heavy maintenance work. Galatasaray played Saturday’s victory over Samsunspor at Basaksehir Fatih Terim stadium, a significantly smaller ground named after the former Turkey manager, who played for and managed Galatasaray.

This ought to have been a magic moment for Pio Esposito. He had just scored his first Serie A hat-trick, becoming only the third Italian to get one for Inter in the era of three points for a win. The last to do it was Christian Vieri, back in 2003. Two years before Esposito was born.

Even if the official November Test window had now closed, as used to be the case, this would already have been a vintage European autumn. Whatever still awaits on the inaugural Nations Championship finals weekend, it has been a richly enjoyable few weeks for both diehard fans and floating voters, topped off by more seismic results and overflowing emotions in London and Dublin on Saturday.

Those flocking to Twickenham had their money’s worth even before the game started, as Lewis Moody, fighting the good fight against motor neurone disease, stood shoulder to shoulder with England’s players as they faced up to the All Blacks’ haka. A record-breaking 37-12 home win was then swiftly followed by Ireland defeating the world champion Springboks 20-17 to complete another resounding northern hemisphere double whammy.

The titles of ATP world No 1 and the best male tennis player in the world are carried by two different names. This has always been clear throughout this messy, injury-ravaged men’s season but it was underlined in the grand finale as Carlos Alcaraz ended his campaign with a statement victory, defeating the top-ranked player, Alexander Zverev, 6-2, 7-6 (7) to win the ATP Finals for the first time.

So much of Alcaraz’s fortunes this season were defined by the wrist injury that forced him out for four and a half months during the spring and summer. No matter, he still managed to tick the two most important items off his to-do list this year.

items.title: Kildunne returns to haunt Harlequins as Bristol get PWR season off to a flyer
items.summary:
• Harlequins 21-48 Bristol

  • Full-back marks debut with two tries against former club

As women’s rugby grows, more scrutiny will follow and Ellie Kildunne has felt that over the past few months. Her performances have been put under a microscope and she was dropped to the bench in England’s final two WXV matches in October, but she silenced her critics with a stellar and trademark performance in her Bristol debut. The full-back did it under significant pressure too, as she returned to the Stoop five months after her shock exit from Harlequins and helped Bristol beat her former side in their Premiership Women’s Rugby opener.

The Bristol head coach, Scott Lawson, had thrown his full backing behind Kildunne in the buildup, saying that being at the West Country club would “bring the best” out of the 27-year-old, and if her debut is anything to go by he will be proved right. The World Cup winner not only scored two tries but was also a linchpin in Bristol’s attack. Her gamechanging reputation was felt among her former teammates as she drew multiple defenders to her whenever she had the ball, meaning the wings on her outside had a lot more joy. The back three looked formidable with both wings, Reneeqa Bonner and Millie David, also scoring two tries apiece.

Watchwithrassie.com had been the surprise internet sensation of the week. Logging on a few hours before South Africa kicked off against Ireland on Saturday, one thing was immediately clear. When it came to rugby’s latest scandal – “RassieGate 3.0” as Bryan Habana called it – this was not a place for balanced debate.

Rassie Erasmus’s “match-fixing” rant, in the aftermath of the Springboks’ defeat by France in Paris, had caused a depressingly familiar furore and earned him a six-match World Rugby ban. Steve Borthwick and Fabien Galthié, among countless others, had made their views known.
